title: Capex on Trial, the Fed on Mute
headline: With the Fed in its quiet period, Meta's spending plan, the 20-year auction and $99 oil decide whether last week's tech rout spreads or stalls.
body:
### Setting the scene

The market walks into the week with a split personality. The S&P 500 fell 1.9% last week to 7,659, yet it is still up 11.9% for the year and only 2.4% below its 52-week high. The damage sat in the AI trade: the Nasdaq-100 lost 5.5% and semiconductors (SMH) 10.5%. The average stock barely noticed. Equal weight (RSP) rose 0.5% and consumer staples (XLP) 5.0%.

The macro inputs are not friendly. WTI closed Friday at $99.02, up 7.8% on the week and 72% this year; Brent finished at $109.86. The 10-year Treasury yields 5.09%, the 2-year 4.74%. The VIX jumped to 20.0 from 16.5 on Friday alone. And the Fed is out of the conversation: the October 27–28 meeting puts it in its pre-meeting quiet period from Saturday, October 17, so there are no Fed speakers on the calendar this week. Earnings, auctions and oil will do the talking.

### The big three questions

1. **Does AI capex still have a buyer?** Meta reports Wednesday with consensus at $6.58 a share on $63.3 billion of revenue; Tesla, the same day, at $0.45 on $27.9 billion. Lam Research and Texas Instruments also report Wednesday, after SMH's 10.5% drop. The beat matters less than next year's spending plan. A Meta capex guide that holds or rises says last week was digestion. A trim says the cycle is turning, and the Nasdaq-100 has further to fall.
2. **Will real money buy the long end at 5%-plus?** The 10-year fell 15bp last week while stocks sold off. Wednesday's 20-year auction last cleared at 5.42%; Thursday's 5-year TIPS at 1.955%. A sloppy 20-year tail would tell us the rally was short-covering.
3. **How far does $99 oil travel?** It shows up first abroad: UK CPI Wednesday (3.4% expected, 3.1% prior), Canada CPI Monday (3.2% expected, 3.0% prior) and Japan CPI late Thursday (2.3% expected, 1.9% prior). At home, Friday's flash PMIs (composite 57.6 expected, 58.4 prior) show whether costs are eating into activity.

### Day by day

| Day | Data and events | Earnings |
|---|---|---|
| Mon Oct 19 | China Q3 GDP (4.4% y/y expected, 4.3% prior), industrial production (5.4%, 5.2%), retail sales (0.5%, 0.4%); Canada CPI (3.2%, 3.0%); Bank of Canada business survey; NAHB index (31, 32) | Steel Dynamics, Zions, Fifth Third, Western Alliance |
| Tue Oct 20 | China loan prime rates (3.0% and 3.5%, hold expected); US housing starts (1.30m, 1.275m) and permits (1.40m, 1.403m); pending home sales (−0.4% m/m, +0.3%); UK unemployment (5.0%, 4.9%); German ZEW (31.6, 34.7) | General Motors, RTX, Netflix, GE Aerospace, Capital One, Northrop Grumman, United Airlines, 3M, KeyCorp |
| Wed Oct 21 | UK CPI (3.4%, 3.1%); EIA crude stocks (prior −8.6m barrels); 20-year bond auction (5.42% prior); Lagarde and Bailey speak | **Meta**, **Tesla**, Elevance Health, AT&T, IBM, Lam Research, Texas Instruments, Thermo Fisher |
| Thu Oct 22 | Jobless claims (200k, 199k); leading index (−0.2%, −0.1%); euro area consumer confidence (−16.0, −16.5); 5-year TIPS auction (1.955% prior); Japan CPI after the US close (2.3%, 1.9%) | Procter & Gamble, Comcast, Lockheed Martin, Union Pacific, Valero, Honeywell, Newmont, Huntington |
| Fri Oct 23 | Flash PMIs: US composite (57.6, 58.4), euro area (52.3, 53.1), Germany (53.0, 53.8), UK (51.7, 52.0); UK retail sales (−0.2% m/m, +0.5%); Canada retail sales | American Express, SLB |

Consensus and prior from FMP's calendars; 76 S&P 500 companies report this week.

### What we're watching, by market

- **US equities:** the model's equity calls get a live test. Regional banks are its top preference and Zions, Fifth Third, KeyCorp and Huntington report. Aerospace and defense is an avoid, and RTX, Northrop and Lockheed all report. Last week's breadth (equal weight up, cap weight down) is the trade we want to keep owning; we would not chase a Meta bounce in the Nasdaq-100.
- **Rates:** the 2-year at 4.74% sits 74bp above the top of the 3.75%–4.00% funds range, so the market already leans toward tighter policy. The 10-year real yield is 2.78% and the 10-year breakeven 2.35%. That is why the model's largest fixed income tilt is a 7% overweight in TIPS: breakevens look cheap against $99 oil.
- **Credit:** the cracks are in the basement. High-yield spreads widened to 3.23% as of Thursday from 2.70% a month earlier; CCC spreads rose about 200bp to 12.78% over the same span. CCC bonds are down 5.2% this year while BBs are up 0.3% and Bs 1.2%. Stay up in quality.
- **Commodities:** Wednesday's inventory report follows an 8.6-million-barrel draw. Valero and SLB give the industry's view of margins and drilling. Oil and gas E&P, a model preference, trades at its 52-week high.
- **International:** China's GDP print sets the tone for emerging markets after EEM's 5.9% drop last week. The UK, another model preference, releases jobs, CPI and retail sales in four days; a hot CPI would push gilt yields higher and test that call.

### Looking further out

The following week is the heavyweight round:

- **Mon Oct 26 and Tue Oct 27:** 2-year (4.787% prior) and 5-year (5.033% prior) note auctions; durable goods; Conference Board confidence (81.9 prior).
- **Wed Oct 28:** the FOMC decides; consensus is a hold at 3.75%–4.00%. The Bank of Canada decides (2.25%). Microsoft and Alphabet report.
- **Thu Oct 29:** Q3 GDP (3.1% expected, 2.2% prior) and September PCE (core 3.3% y/y expected, 3.0% prior); the ECB decides (deposit rate 2.50%); 7-year auction; Amazon, Eli Lilly, Caterpillar and Intel report.
- **Fri Oct 30:** the Bank of Japan decides (1.25%); employment cost index; euro area Q3 GDP; Exxon and Chevron report. Apple follows on November 2.

### Bottom line

We read last week as a rotation inside a bull market, and we give that view 60% odds. The dashboard agrees in its own way: 67% equities against a 60% neutral, with its favorites in regional banks, oil and gas producers and the UK. Its live record began with the first saved call on October 17; no session has closed since, so there is nothing to score yet. What would change our mind is credit. If high-yield spreads push through 3.50% while Meta trims its spending plan, we would cut equity risk and add to Treasuries and TIPS. Until then, own breadth, own quality credit, and let the megacaps prove themselves.

title: The Generals Retreated, the Troops Held
headline: The S&P 500 fell 2.0% as chips sank 10.5%, but the equal-weighted index rose and bonds rallied: a rotation inside a bull market, with a warning light in CCC credit.
body:
### The week in one paragraph

The S&P 500 fell 2.0% in its worst week since June, but the damage was concentrated. The Nasdaq-100 lost 5.5% and semiconductors 10.5%, while the equal-weighted S&P 500 *rose* 0.5% and Russell 1000 Value gained 0.9%. Consumer staples (+5.0%), energy (+4.9%) and health care (+3.5%) led. This was a rotation, not a rout: the generals retreated while the troops held their ground. Bonds did their job again, with the 10-year Treasury yield down 12bp to 5.10% as stocks slid. The VIX jumped 35% to 20.0, which is elevated but not panicked.

### Scoreboard

| Market | Level | Week | Year to date |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 (SPY) | 763.25 | −2.0% | +12.8% |
| Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) | 709.80 | −5.5% | +15.9% |
| S&P 500 equal weight (RSP) | 214.09 | +0.5% | +13.1% |
| Russell 1000 Value (IWD) | 255.77 | +0.9% | +22.9% |
| Russell 1000 Growth (IWF) | 121.48 | −5.0% | +2.9% |
| Russell 2000 (IWM) | 270.44 | −3.1% | +10.6% |
| Developed ex-US (EFA) | 103.55 | +0.2% | +9.5% |
| Emerging markets (EEM) | 62.85 | −5.9% | +15.5% |
| 10-year Treasury | 5.10% | −12bp | +92bp |
| High yield (HYG) | 76.86 | −0.5% | −0.3% |
| WTI crude | $99.02 | +7.8% | +72.5% |
| Gold | $4,181 | −0.8% | −3.7% |
| Dollar index | 101.66 | −0.4% | +3.7% |

### Chips down, staples up

The AI complex finally ran into the law of high expectations. ASML beat consensus EPS by 19% and TSMC by 3%, yet SMH dropped 10.5% and technology 7.7%. When beats get sold, the bar has moved above what even excellent results can clear. Korea, the market's purest memory-chip play, fell 15.1%.

We don't read this as the end of the AI cycle. Capex intentions on earnings calls are still rising, and AI and data centers came up on 81% of S&P 500 calls last season, against 69% a year earlier. What it does tell us is that leadership is broadening. The equal-weighted index beat the cap-weighted one by about 2.5 points in a single week. That's healthy for the bull market and painful for anyone overweight the top ten.

### Inflation: hot at the pump, cool underneath

- **Consumer prices:** September CPI rose 0.6% m/m and 3.7% y/y, as oil near $100 worked through. Core CPI rose 0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y, which is not alarming.
- **Pipeline:** producer prices were the hot spot, up 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, with core PPI up 0.7%. Import prices rose 1.1% m/m.
- **What bonds believe:** the 10-year breakeven is 2.35%, up only 7bp over the past year even as crude has roughly doubled. The market is treating the energy shock as a level shift, not a new inflation regime.
- **Who did the tightening:** the 10-year TIPS real yield rose 102bp over the year to 2.78%. Real rates are doing the Fed's work.

### Growth: no recession in these numbers

Headline retail sales rose just 0.1%, but sales ex-autos rose 0.9% and the year-on-year pace is 6.3% nominal. Industrial production jumped 0.7%, the Empire State survey surged to 25.5 (10.3 expected), and jobless claims held at 199,000. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow puts Q3 at 3.6%. The Philly Fed's slide to 20.9 from 37.8, with new orders down to 4.3, is the one soft spot worth watching.

### The Fed: Warsh keeps his options open

The Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023, and the median dot shows one more in December. This week Chair Warsh declined to pre-commit, and traders scaled back bets on an October hike. With core CPI at 2.6% and real yields near 2.8%, the case for a second hike is weaker than the September dots suggested. The FOMC announces its decision on October 28.

### Credit: watch the bottom of the stack

Investment grade spreads barely moved, at 84bp. High yield widened 8bp on the week and 47bp over the month to 323bp. CCC spreads blew out 193bp in a month to 1,278bp, within a few basis points of their widest in three years. The weakest borrowers are feeling 5% Treasury yields first. Year to date, CCCs are down 5.2% while BBs are up 0.3%. That divergence is our main risk flag.

### Earnings season: off to a strong start

Financials set a high bar:

- **Beats:** Goldman Sachs (EPS $17.01 vs $12.86 expected), BlackRock (+11%), Citigroup (+7%), Morgan Stanley (+3%), UnitedHealth (+13%), Johnson & Johnson (+3%).
- **Misses:** JPMorgan (−3%) and Bank of America (−2%), both modest.

The season's first 31 S&P 500 calls are running more upbeat than a year ago. Last season, 25% of companies mentioned raising guidance against 17% a year earlier.

### What the model says

The dashboard's allocation models still favor equities modestly: 67% against a 60% neutral, up from 66% a month ago. In fixed income they overweight TIPS and EM local-currency bonds against the Agg. In equities they prefer:

- **Regional banks:** 1.2× book value.
- **Oil & gas E&P:** at its 52-week high.
- **The UK:** 5.7% shareholder yield.
- **Global ex-US:** 11.3× forward earnings.

They avoid metals & mining, aerospace & defense and consumer discretionary. This week's rotation went the model's way.

### Bottom line

Our read is a rotation within a bull market, not the start of a bear market. Earnings are strong, the economy is running near 3.5% real growth, and long-run inflation expectations are anchored. The risks are 5% long yields, $100 oil and a CCC market that is cracking. We would use AI weakness to rebalance toward the broader market rather than to chase it lower, and keep a close eye on high yield.
